title: Section 1.8: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 (Workbook p. 23)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Literal Equations & Formulas (Workbook p. 23)
- **Literal Equation / Formula:** An equation containing **multiple variables** ($a, b, x, y, r, t$).
- **Solving for a Specified Variable:** Isolating that target variable completely on one side.
- **Strategy:** Treat all other letters exactly like known constants/numbers!
$$\text{If you would subtract 5, subtract } x\text{! If you would divide by 3, divide by } m\text{!}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Reminder:** The rules do NOT change just because letters are involved. Use the exact same properties of equality!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 14 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is TA Sora. Today, we turn to Section 1.8 on workbook pages 23 and 24: Solving Formulas for a Specified VariableâLiteral Equations. Hello everyone!

[TA Sora] Up until today, most equations had one letter (like x) and several numbers (like 3x + 5 = 20). Today, we encounter formulas that contain MULTIPLE variablesâlike d = rt, P = 2L + 2W, or Ax + By = C.

[Prof. Park] These are called literal equations or formulas because they are written with letters ('litera' in Latin). Students are often intimidated by literal equations because there aren't many numbers to calculate.

[TA Sora] They ask: 'How can I solve for y if I don't know what x or z equals?'
The secret is simple: Treat all other letters exactly like known constants!

[Prof. Park] Ask yourself: 'If that letter were the number 5, what operation would I use to move it?' If you would subtract 5, then subtract x! If you would divide by 3, then divide by m! The algebraic rules never changeâonly the symbols do!

[TA Sora] In real Montana careers, you do this all the time: In agriculture, irrigation water rights formulas are solved for flow duration t. In forestry and wildlife biology, timber board-foot formulas are solved for usable log diameter d.

[Prof. Park] In construction across Gallatin County, perimeter and load formulas are rearranged to calculate beam length L. Today, we will master isolating any target variable with 100% confidence. Let's begin on slide 2! In civil engineering, environmental science, and business management, real equations are almost always literal formulas.

[TA Sora] For example, the Manning formula calculates open-channel water velocity in irrigation canals across the Gallatin Valley based on channel slope, roughness, and hydraulic radius.

[Prof. Park] An engineer rarely needs to solve for velocity; they already know the target water flow rate, and they need to solve for the channel slope S or roughness coefficient n! Rearranging formulas is the daily bread and butter of working professionals.

[TA Sora] That is why literal equations are so empowering. Once you isolate a formula for your target variable, you can plug in twenty different datasets into a spreadsheet and compute answers instantly without re-doing algebra every single time!

title: Example 1A & 1B: Solving Linear Equations for y
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 Example 1A & 1B (Workbook p. 23)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each formula for y (Workbook p. 23)
$$\text{A. } 3x + y = 8$$
$$\text{B. } 2x - 5y = 12$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ A:}\quad & \text{Isolate } y \text{ by subtracting } 3x \text{ from both sides:} \\
& 3x + y - 3x = 8 - 3x \\
& \mathbf{y = 8 - 3x} \quad (\text{or } \mathbf{y = -3x + 8}) \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ B:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Subtract } 2x: \\
& -5y = 12 - 2x \\
& \text{Step 2: Divide by } -5: \\
& y = \frac{12 - 2x}{-5} = \mathbf{\frac{2x - 12}{5}} \quad \left(\text{or } \mathbf{y = \frac{2}{5}x - \frac{12}{5}}\right)
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Dividing by a Negative:** In 1B, dividing by $-5$ flips the signs in the numerator: $\frac{12 - 2x}{-5} = \frac{2x - 12}{5}$. Both forms are correct!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 2, let's examine Section 1.8 Examples 1A and 1B on workbook page 23: Solving standard linear equations for y. Part A: 3x + y = 8. Part B: 2x - 5y = 12. In Part A, we want to isolate y: 3x + y = 8.

[TA Sora] Look at what is on the same side as y: we have a positive 3x added to y. To eliminate +3x, what is the inverse operation? Subtract 3x from both sides! 3x + y - 3x = 8 - 3x.

[Prof. Park] On the left, 3x - 3x = 0, leaving y isolated! On the right: Can you combine 8 and -3x into 5x? ABSOLUTELY NOT! 8 is a constant and -3x has a variableâthey are NOT like terms!

[TA Sora] You simply write them side-by-side: y = 8 - 3x (or y = -3x + 8). Done in one step! Now let's solve Part B: 2x - 5y = 12. We want to isolate y.

[Prof. Park] Step 1: Get the y term (-5y) alone by subtracting 2x from both sides: -5y = 12 - 2x (or -5y = -2x + 12). Step 2: y is multiplied by -5. Divide BOTH sides by -5: y = (-2x + 12) / (-5).

[TA Sora] Now distribute the division by -5 to both terms: -2x / -5 = +(2/5)x. +12 / -5 = -12/5. So y = (2/5)x - 12/5 (or (2x - 12) / 5). Notice that dividing by -5 changed the signs upstairs: -2x became positive 2x, and +12 became -12.

[Prof. Park] This formây = mx + bâis the famous slope-intercept form we will use extensively in Unit 2! In Example 1B, 2x - 5y = 12, we isolated y to get y = (2/5)x - 12/5.

[TA Sora] Notice why we split the fraction into two separate terms: In Unit 2, we will graph linear equations using the slope-intercept form: y = mx + b.

[Prof. Park] Here, m = 2/5 is the slope (the steepness of the line: rise 2, run 5), and b = -12/5 is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the vertical axis)! Solving literal equations for y is the exact skill that unlocks all of linear graphing in Unit 2!

[TA Sora] Every topic in Unit 1 is purposefully laying the groundwork for Unit 2. Practice this isolation until it is second nature!

title: Example 1C & 1D: Solving for Factored & Monomial Variables
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 Example 1C & 1D (Workbook p. 23)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each formula for y (Workbook p. 23)
$$\text{C. } Z = x + wxy$$
$$\text{D. } 5xy = 19$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Subtract } x \text{ to isolate the } y\text{-term:} \\
& Z - x = wxy \\
& \text{Step 2: Divide both sides by the coefficients of } y \text{, which are } wx: \\
& \mathbf{y = \frac{Z - x}{wx}} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Divide both sides by } 5x: \\
& \mathbf{y = \frac{19}{5x}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Multi-Variable Coefficients:** In 1C, $w$ and $x$ are multiplying $y$. To isolate $y$, divide by the entire package $wx$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 3 covers Section 1.8 Examples 1C and 1D on workbook page 23: Part C: Z = x + wxy; solve for y. Part D: 5xy = 19; solve for y. Look at Part C: Z = x + wxy. We want to isolate y.

[TA Sora] Notice where y lives: y is inside the term wxy! Step 1: Isolate the term containing y. Subtract x from both sides: Z - x = wxy. Step 2: What is multiplying y? Both w and x are multiplying y: (wx) Â· y!

[Prof. Park] The inverse of multiplying by wx is dividing by wx! Divide both sides by wx: (Z - x) / (wx) = y. So y = (Z - x) / (wx)! Can we cancel the x in the numerator with the x in the denominator? NO!

[TA Sora] Z - x is a subtraction! You can only cancel common factors, never terms attached by minus! Now look at Part D: 5xy = 19. Solve for y. y is multiplied by 5 and x: (5x) Â· y = 19.

[Prof. Park] To isolate y in one step, divide both sides by 5x: y = 19 / (5x). Simple, direct, and completely isolated! Let's look closely at Part C: Z = x + wxy; solve for y.

[TA Sora] Notice why students fail this problem: they try to divide by wx before subtracting x! If you divide by wx first, you would have to divide the x term as well: Z/(wx) = x/(wx) + y. That creates a fraction mess!

[Prof. Park] Always isolate the entire term containing your target variable FIRST by adding or subtracting non-target terms, and ONLY THEN divide by the coefficient factors! Isolate the term first, then isolate the variable! That two-step rhythm guarantees success every time.

[TA Sora] Remember our classroom motto: discipline with steps yields effortless accuracy on exams!

[TA Sora] Exactly! Take it line by line, check each arithmetic move, and celebrate every victory!

title: Example 2A & 2B: Solving for Specified Variable b
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 Example 2A & 2B (Workbook p. 23)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each literal equation for the specified variable (Workbook p. 23)
$$\text{A. } a + b - c = d; \quad \text{solve for } b$$
$$\text{B. } ax^2 + bx + c = 0; \quad \text{solve for } b$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ A:}\quad & \text{Subtract } a \text{ and add } c \text{ to both sides:} \\
& b = d - a + c \\
& \mathbf{b = d - a + c} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ B:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Move all non-}b \text{ terms to the right side:} \\
& bx = -ax^2 - c \\
& \text{Step 2: Divide both sides by } x: \\
& \mathbf{b = \frac{-ax^2 - c}{x}} \quad \left(\text{or } \mathbf{b = -ax - \frac{c}{x}}\right)
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Treating Terms as Blocks:** In 2B, $ax^2$ and $c$ have no $b$. Move them as complete units over to the right side!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 4, let's examine Section 1.8 Examples 2A and 2B on workbook page 23: Solving for specified variable b: Part A: a + b - c = d; solve for b. Part B: ax^2 + bx + c = 0; solve for b.

[TA Sora] In Part A: a + b - c = d. We want to isolate b. What is attached to b? We have +a and -c. To undo +a, subtract a from both sides. To undo -c, add c to both sides!

[Prof. Park] So b = d - a + c! Notice that every term moved across the equal sign simply took its opposite sign: +a became -a, and -c became +c! Now look at Part B: ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Solve for b.

[TA Sora] This looks like the general quadratic equation from advanced algebra! Our target variable is b, which is inside the middle term bx. Step 1: Isolate the term bx by moving all other terms to the right side: Subtract ax^2 from both sides: -ax^2.

[Prof. Park] Subtract c from both sides: -c. So we get: bx = -ax^2 - c. Step 2: To isolate b, divide both sides by x: b = (-ax^2 - c) / x (or b = -ax - c/x). That is our complete solution for b!

[TA Sora] In Part B: ax^2 + bx + c = 0; solve for b. Notice that x appears with an exponent of 2 in ax^2, but our target is b! Don't worry about the x^2âto variable b, ax^2 is just a single package term!

[Prof. Park] Subtract ax^2, subtract c, and divide by x. Treating non-target variable clusters as single numbers is the mark of a mature algebra student.

[TA Sora] Remember our classroom motto: discipline with steps yields effortless accuracy on exams!

[TA Sora] Exactly! Take it line by line, check each arithmetic move, and celebrate every victory!

title: Example 2C & 2D: Solving Fractional Formulas for r
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 Example 2C & 2D (Workbook p. 24)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each formula for r (Workbook p. 24)
$$\text{C. } m = \frac{r - 7n}{5}; \quad \text{solve for } r$$
$$\text{D. } t = \frac{d}{r}; \quad \text{solve for } r$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Multiply both sides by } 5: \\
& 5m = r - 7n \\
& \text{Step 2: Add } 7n \text{ to both sides:} \\
& \mathbf{r = 5m + 7n} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Target } r \text{ is in the denominator! Multiply by } r \text{ first:} \\
& r \cdot t = d \\
& \text{Now divide by } t: \\
& \mathbf{r = \frac{d}{t}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Variable in Denominator Trap:** In 2D, you CANNOT solve for $r$ while it is trapped in the bottom! Multiply by $r$ first to bring it upstairs: $rt = d \implies r = \frac{d}{t}$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 presents Section 1.8 Examples 2C and 2D on workbook page 24: Solving fractional formulas for r: Part C: m = (r - 7n) / 5; solve for r. Part D: t = d / r; solve for r.

[TA Sora] Look at Part C: m = (r - 7n) / 5. Our target is r, but r is trapped inside a fraction! How do we free r from the fraction? Clear the fraction!

[Prof. Park] Multiply both sides by the denominator 5: 5 Â· m = 5 Â· [ (r - 7n) / 5 ]. On the right, the 5 cancels, leaving: 5m = r - 7n. Now add 7n to both sides to isolate r: r = 5m + 7n!

[TA Sora] Multiplying by the denominator first immediately freed our variable! Now look at Part D: t = d / r. Solve for r. This is the famous distance, rate, and time formula from physics: time = distance / rate!

[Prof. Park] For example, driving 90 miles on Interstate 90 from Bozeman to Butte at speed r takes time t. Notice where r is: r is trapped DOWNSTAIRS in the denominator! You can NEVER solve for a variable while it is in the denominator!

[TA Sora] Step 1: Get r out of the basement! Multiply both sides by r: r Â· t = r Â· (d / r) = d. So we get: rt = d (distance = rate times time).

[Prof. Park] Step 2: Now that r is upstairs, isolate r by dividing both sides by t: r = d / t! Speed equals distance divided by time. Clean, intuitive, and physically meaningful! Let's look at the physics formula in Part D: t = d / r.

[TA Sora] If you drive from Bozeman to Billings on Interstate 90, the distance d is about 142 miles. If you want to make the trip in t = 2 hours, what average speed r must you maintain?

[Prof. Park] Using our solved formula r = d / t: r = 142 / 2 = 71 miles per hour! Formulas give you direct control over real physical decisions. And notice the common pitfall: students see t = d/r and write r = d Â· t!

[TA Sora] Remember: since r was in the denominator, multiplying by r brings it to the numerator on the other side: rt = d. Then dividing by t gives r = d/t!

title: Example 2E & 2F: Geometric Formulas for W
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 Example 2E & 2F (Workbook p. 24)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each geometry formula for W (Workbook p. 24)
$$\text{E. } P = 2L + 2W; \quad \text{solve for } W$$
$$\text{F. } V = LWH; \quad \text{solve for } W$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ E\ (Perimeter):}\quad & \text{Step 1: Subtract } 2L \text{ from both sides:} \\
& P - 2L = 2W \\
& \text{Step 2: Divide by } 2: \\
& \mathbf{W = \frac{P - 2L}{2}} \quad \left(\text{or } \mathbf{W = \frac{P}{2} - L}\right) \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ F\ (Volume):}\quad & \text{Divide both sides by } LH: \\
& \mathbf{W = \frac{V}{LH}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Don't Cancel the 2 Illegally!** In Part E, $\frac{P - 2L}{2} \neq P - L$! The 2 divides the ENTIRE numerator, so it becomes $\frac{P}{2} - L$!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 6, we explore geometric formulas from workbook page 24: Part E: P = 2L + 2W; solve for W. Part F: V = LWH; solve for W. Part E is the perimeter formula for a rectangle: Perimeter = 2 times Length + 2 times Width.

[TA Sora] Imagine fencing a horse pasture in the Gallatin Valley: you know the total perimeter fencing P you bought, and you know the pasture length L. How wide can the pasture be? We must solve for W!

[Prof. Park] Step 1: Isolate the 2W term by subtracting 2L from both sides: P - 2L = 2W. Step 2: Divide both sides by 2: W = (P - 2L) / 2 (or W = P/2 - L).

[TA Sora] Can the 2 in 2L cancel with the 2 in the denominator? NO! P is not multiplied by 2! You cannot cancel unless BOTH terms share the factor 2! Now look at Part F: V = LWH. Solve for W.

[Prof. Park] This is the volume formula for a rectangular prism (like a timber beam or concrete foundation footer): Volume = Length times Width times Height. W is multiplied by both L and H: (LH) Â· W = V.

[TA Sora] To isolate W, divide both sides by LH: W = V / (LH)! Width equals volume divided by the product of length and height. In Part E: P = 2L + 2W; solve for W.

[Prof. Park] Let's see the pasture fencing example with real numbers: Suppose a Gallatin rancher has P = 1,000 feet of wooden post fencing and wants the pasture length to be L = 300 feet.

[TA Sora] Using our formula W = (P - 2L) / 2: W = (1000 - 2(300)) / 2 = (1000 - 600) / 2 = 400 / 2 = 200 feet! The pasture width must be 200 feet. Formula rearranged once, solved in ten seconds!

[Prof. Park] That is the beauty of applied mathematics.

title: Section 1.8 Review: Solving Equations by Clearing Fractions
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 14 • Section 1.8 Review A & B (Workbook p. 24)
detail: Lecture 14: Solving Formulas for a Specified Variable (Literal Equations)
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### REVIEW: Solve the following equations by clearing fractions (Workbook p. 24)
$$\text{A. } \frac{y - 2}{5} = \frac{3}{2}y + \frac{4}{5}$$
$$\text{B. } \frac{2}{7} = \frac{3}{7}(x - 4) - \frac{5}{7}$$
pitfall: **Multiplying Binomial Numerator:** In Review A, $10 \div 5 = 2$, which must distribute to $(y - 2)$ to make $2y - 4$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 7 concludes Lecture 14 with our Section 1.8 Review Problems from workbook page 24: Solving equations by clearing fractions: Review A: (y - 2) / 5 = (3/2)y + 4/5. Review B: 2/7 = (3/7)(x - 4) - 5/7.

[TA Sora] Let's solve Review A: (y - 2) / 5 = (3/2)y + 4/5. Look at the denominators: 5, 2, and 5. The LCD is 10!

[Prof. Park] Multiply every term by 10: 10 Â· [ (y - 2) / 5 ] = 10 Â· [ (3/2)y ] + 10 Â· [ 4/5 ]. First term: 10 / 5 = 2, so 2(y - 2) = 2y - 4. Second term: 10 Â· (3/2) = 15y.

[TA Sora] Third term: 10 Â· (4/5) = 8. So we get: 2y - 4 = 15y + 8. Subtract 2y from both sides: -4 = 13y + 8. Subtract 8 from both sides: -12 = 13y. Divide by 13: y = -12/13!

[Prof. Park] Now let's solve Review B: 2/7 = (3/7)(x - 4) - 5/7. All denominators are 7, so the LCD is 7! Multiply every term by 7: 2 = 3(x - 4) - 5. Distribute: 2 = 3x - 12 - 5.

[TA Sora] Combine like terms: 2 = 3x - 17. Add 17 to both sides: 19 = 3x. Divide by 3: x = 19/3! In Lecture 15, we conclude Unit 1 with Section 1.9: Solving Linear Inequalities and Interval Notation! Fantastic work today, and see you in Lecture 15!

[Prof. Park] In Review Problem A: (y - 2)/5 = (3/2)y + 4/5, we multiplied by LCD = 10 to get 2(y - 2) = 15y + 8, leading to y = -12/13.

[TA Sora] Notice how literal equations and clearing fractions reinforce each other: Both skills require identifying the structural anatomy of an equation and systematically peeling away outer operations. In Lecture 15, we will conclude Unit 1 with inequalities!
